newsitem.title: JAPAN: French franc tumbles in Asia after leftist victory.
newsitem.headline: French franc tumbles in Asia after leftist victory.

text.p: The French franc fell versus the German mark in Asia on Monday following the French Socialists' election win, but dealers here and in Singapore said its drop was cushioned by talk of intervention by the Bank of France.

"The market believes that the Banque de France is holding their hands on top (capping franc/mark rates). They're said to be in a little bit here and there, at 3.3850, 3.3900 (per mark)," a European bank dealer in Singapore said.
"But the market itself is looking for a move up to the 3.4000 level, so we might have a slow move up there," he said.
The franc was at 3.3845/50 per mark at 0525 GMT, compared with Friday's levels of about 3.3775 in late New York and 3.3810 in London.

"We (the mark) opened higher than New York's close, but it looks like the Banque de France has been in all day through various counter-parties and they've really provided the liquidity that the market's needed and taken the sting out of it," said another European bank dealer in Singapore.
Tokyo dealers said the Bank of France has had offers in place at 3.3820 since last week and talk circulated in Tokyo that it sold marks at 3.3800 in early Asia trade on Monday.
The result of the French parliamentary election was a major defeat for President Jacques Chirac's centre-right coalition, which lost almost half the 464 seats it held in the outgoing Lower House.

"As soon as people saw last week that it looked as if the Left were going to get in, they bought mark/French from the low of 3.3700, so most of the buying was made before the results came. Maybe the size of the victory was a little bit of a surprise, but not much else," said another Singapore dealer.
A further fall in the French franc against the mark is possible later in Europe if French stock and bond markets are battered by the election results, Tokyo dealers said.
"There is no reason for the franc to be bought because stocks and bonds there would probably be hurt by the election results," said a dealer at a French bank in Tokyo.
He added that, while the focus is on how far the French franc will fall, talk of intervention by the Bank of France will emerge every time mark/French franc rates rise.

But a dealer at a European bank in Tokyo said it was not clear whether the mark's rise against the franc would be sustained, as the mark has also come under selling pressure against currencies such as the U.S. dollar and the yen.

Growing concerns about enlarged membership of the European economic and monetary union and a weak euro, as well as conflict between the Bundesbank and the Bonn government over the revaluation of the German central bank's gold reserves, have weighed on the mark.
